citation: Morel, G. M. (2021). Student-centered learning: context needed. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09951-0
title: Own It, Learn It, Share It framework for student-centered learning
description: Lee and Hannafin's design framework "intersects constructivist, constructionist, and self-determination theories to address student-centered learning." It has three parts: "Own It involves students developing ownership over the process and achieving personally meaningful learning goals," Learn It involves autonomous learning "through metacognitive, procedural, conceptual, and strategic scaffolding," and Share It involves students generating "artifacts aimed at authentic audiences beyond the classroom assessment." The framework also includes "ten discrete design guidelines for the instructional design process."
requirements: The framework is described as combining constructivist, constructionist, and self-determination theories
constraints: Cheng notes it is a time-consuming, general approach rather than an efficient, customizable approach in times of restricted resources
target_learners: students in digital and online learning contexts
examples: Baird applied the framework as a blueprint to a flexible assignment designed to promote intrinsic motivation and engagement
key_sources: Morel, G. M. (2021). Student-centered learning: context needed. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09951-0

article_title: Response to “A design framework for enhancing engagement in student-centered learning: own it, learn it, and share it”: a design perspective
citation: Xiaoqing Gu. (2021). Response to “A design framework for enhancing engagement in student-centered learning: own it, learn it, and share it”: a design perspective. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09896-w
title: Lee and Hannafin's own it, learn it, and share it design framework for enhancing engagement in student-centered learning, revisited from a design perspective
description: This response essay revisits the design framework that Lee and Hannafin published in 2016 for "enhancing engagement in student-centered learning," which the abstract names by its three-part motto "own it, learn it, and share it." The essay discusses the framework's "value, application, and future development" in light of the pandemic-era move to full-scale online teaching. The detailed framework content appears in the underlying 2016 article rather than in the visible portion of this essay.
requirements: The essay treats the framework as applicable to student-centered learning in online teaching and learning practice, where learners own, learn, and share their learning.
constraints: The visible abstract does not print the framework's internal design details; the essay is a response commentary rather than a restatement of the framework.
target_learners: students in online and technology-supported learning environments
examples: The author revisited the 2016 Lee and Hannafin article and discussed its value, application, and future development as a response to a special issue call on shifting to digital.
key_sources: Xiaoqing Gu. (2021). Response to “A design framework for enhancing engagement in student-centered learning: own it, learn it, and share it”: a design perspective. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09896-w

article_title: Chaos: exploring an engaging online model for rapid application during the pandemic
citation: Joshua W. Tabor. (2020). Chaos: exploring an engaging online model for rapid application during the pandemic. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09878-y
title: The Own it, Learn it, Share it framework structures student-centered online learning in three steps
description: Tabor describes Lee and Hannafin's framework as a three-step student-centered course design built on self-determination theory, constructivism, and constructionism. In 'own it', students set their own goals; in 'learn it', teachers support them through direct instruction, tools, resources or discourse; in 'share it', students present a completed artifact to a selected group for feedback. Each step is designed to provide support as students explore topics interesting to them with a tangible product evaluated upon completion.
requirements: Teachers must understand the rationale behind each step of the framework, which the authors support with multiple examples explaining the 'why'
constraints: Applying the outline may be difficult due to a possible lack of understanding of student-centered learning techniques, lack of time to train teachers, and possibly teacher apathy towards online education
target_learning_goals: Student engagement and lifelong learning in digital, student-centered environments
examples: Tabor proposes schools let teachers practice with the framework and set expectations that some, if not all, of it be followed when planning for the upcoming year
key_sources: Joshua W. Tabor. (2020). Chaos: exploring an engaging online model for rapid application during the pandemic. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09878-y

citation: Noah S. Podolefsky. (2013). Intentional Design for Empowerment. https://arxiv.org/abs/1306.6544
title: Ownership of the means of production of knowledge (Marx adapted to learning)
description: The article adapts Marx's concept of ownership of the means of production to learning, following Lave and McDermott's reading of Estranged Labor: "when learners lose ownership over the means of production of knowledge, they become alienated from both the product and process of learning," and enter competitive rather than cooperative relations with teachers and peers. The author uses this lens to argue that many school activities, while productive for content learning, may take ownership from students, and that designers should return ownership of knowledge production to students while still meeting content goals.
requirements: Schooling must pursue established content goals while returning ownership over how knowledge is produced to students, so participants can feel themselves cooperative partners.
constraints: Ownership cannot be established simply by "handing over the reins to students without further reflection": Meno's paradox means learners left on their own may be unable to generate either the answers or the questions.
target_learners: students and teachers across the school system, from K-12 to higher education
examples: The article reads standard guided activities such as introductory physics labs, where nearly all actions are explicitly guided, as practices that may strip students of ownership.
key_sources: Noah S. Podolefsky. (2013). Intentional Design for Empowerment. https://arxiv.org/abs/1308.5956

article_title: Preliminary model for student ownership of projects
citation: Dimitri R. Dounas-Frazer, Laura Ríos, and H. J. Lewandowski (2019). Preliminary model for student ownership of projects. https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.01690
title: Preliminary model of student ownership of projects as a student-project relationship organized by three project phases and three interaction categories
description: The article interprets student ownership of a project as "a type of relationship between student and project" that evolves over time. It visualizes ownership as a grid whose rows are project phases (CHOICE, EXECUTION, SYNTHESIS) and whose columns are student-project interactions (CONTRIBUTIONS, NEW UNDERSTANDING, EMOTIONAL RESPONSES), so that ownership-relevant interactions depend on the project phase. The model was developed from interview transcripts and prior ownership literature.
requirements: Developed through two rounds of consensus coding in which each transcript excerpt was assigned to one of nine phase-by-interaction groups
constraints: The authors state the model is preliminary because they have not yet mapped it to their full data set
target_learning_goals: student ownership of multiweek experimental physics projects
examples: Coding placed excerpts such as a student's account of troubleshooting contributions and an instructor's account of investment in topic choice into the grid's phase-by-interaction groups
key_sources: Dimitri R. Dounas-Frazer, Laura Ríos, and H. J. Lewandowski (2019). Preliminary model for student ownership of projects. https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.01690

article_title: Preliminary model for student ownership of projects
citation: Dimitri R. Dounas-Frazer, Laura Ríos, and H. J. Lewandowski (2019). Preliminary model for student ownership of projects. https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.01690
title: Use a model of student ownership as a reflection tool for instructors and students to make informed decisions about changes to the lab learning environment
description: The article proposes that an ownership model can serve as a practical reflection tool: it "may also be a useful tool for instructors and students alike to reflect on their shared experiences during lab projects and make informed decisions about changes to the learning environment." The grid model supports such reflection by organizing shared project experiences by phase and interaction type.
requirements: A model of ownership grounded in participants' conceptions, such as the article's preliminary grid model
constraints: The article's model is preliminary and not yet mapped to the authors' full data set
target_learners: instructors of upper-division physics lab courses
target_learning_goals: student ownership of multiweek experimental physics projects
examples: The authors state the model could facilitate future studies of ownership in lab courses and possibly other settings
key_sources: Dimitri R. Dounas-Frazer, Laura Ríos, and H. J. Lewandowski (2019). Preliminary model for student ownership of projects. https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.01690

article_title: Studying physics during the COVID-19 pandemic: Student assessments of learning achievement, perceived effectiveness of online recitations, and online laboratories
citation: P. Klein, L. Ivanjek, M.N. Dahlkemper, K. Jeličić, M.-A. Geyer, S. Küchemann, and A. Susac. (2020). Studying physics during the COVID-19 pandemic: Student assessments of learning achievement, perceived effectiveness of online recitations, and online laboratories. https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.05622
title: Design online recitations around graded feedback on students' own solutions and online laboratories around students gathering their own data
description: The article concludes that "graded feedback followed by online discussions turned out to be more eﬀective (in the students' perspective) than handed solutions", and that "students value the possibility of gathering own data" in online physics laboratories. Gathering own data can be accomplished via remote controlled labs or, more easily, videos or simulations of experiments.
requirements: Making the solution process visible (reconstruction) requires technical resources, e.g. tablet computer with pen input
Gathering own data from a distance requires remote controlled labs, videos, or simulations from experiments
constraints: When secondhand data is used, the article advises clarifying its origin, e.g. with a detailed description of the measurement including photographs of the experimental setup
target_learners: university physics students in online recitation and laboratory courses
target_learning_goals: problem-solving skills supported by feedback on students' own solutions
experimental skills and content reinforcement through gathering and analyzing own measurement data
examples: In the study, students who sent their own solution to be rated (N = 168) assessed recitation effectiveness significantly higher than students who did not (N = 227).
key_sources: P. Klein, L. Ivanjek, M.N. Dahlkemper, K. Jeličić, M.-A. Geyer, S. Küchemann, and A. Susac. (2020). Studying physics during the COVID-19 pandemic: Student assessments of learning achievement, perceived effectiveness of online recitations, and online laboratories. https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.05622

article_title: Student ownership and understanding of multi-week final projects
citation: Lassen, I. C., Arielle-Evans, A. A., Ríos, L., Lewandowski, H. J., & Dounas-Frazer, D. R. (2021). Student ownership and understanding of multi-week final projects. https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.00111
title: Ownership-as-relationship model of student project ownership
description: The ownership-as-relationship model treats ownership as a dynamic relationship between students and their projects, not a static trait. In the article's own terms, "ownership was modeled as a relationship between students and projects that consists of three types of student-project interactions and evolves across three sequential project phases." The interactions are students' contributions to, emotional responses to, and new knowledge about the project; the phases are choice of topic and team, execution of the research, and creation of deliverables. This paper refines the third phase, renaming synthesis as deliverables, and elaborates the new-understanding interaction across all three phases.
requirements: Students must work in groups of 2–4 on multi-week projects lasting 4–7 weeks in upper-level physics lab courses for the model's phases to be instantiated as described
constraints: The article states that, due to the qualitative design, it cannot make probabilistically generalizable claims and aims instead for theoretical generalizability; phase-less atypical interactions were excluded from the analysis
target_learners: undergraduate students in upper-division physics lab courses
target_learning_goals: developing new knowledge about a project's domain, apparatus, management, and the nature of science
examples: The model was applied as an a priori coding scheme to all 15 interview transcripts, with coders flagging fewer than 6% of about 700 phase-coded and fewer than 12% of about 900 interaction-coded excerpts.
key_sources: Lassen, I. C., Arielle-Evans, A. A., Ríos, L., Lewandowski, H. J., & Dounas-Frazer, D. R. (2021). Student ownership and understanding of multi-week final projects. https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.00111
